facts.fact: The Rashtrakutas were earlier feudatories of the Chalukyas.
Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta kingdom by overthrowing the Chalukya Kirtivarman II.
Krishna I built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
The Kailasa temple is a rock-cut monolith carved top-down.
The Kailasa temple is Dravidian in style, its tiered tower resembling the Mamallapuram rathas.
Govinda III was the most militarily successful Rashtrakuta, conquering from Kanyakumari to Kanauj and defeating Nagabhatta II.
Amoghavarsha I shifted the capital to Manyakheta (Malkhed).
Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada poetic work.
Amoghavarsha I was converted to Jainism by the monk Jinasena.
Jinasena wrote the Adipurana.
Pampa wrote the Vikramarjuna Vijaya.
Ponna wrote the Santipurana.
The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I record Chola local self-government.
Chola village committee members were chosen by lot (kudavolai, pot-ticket).
The wards of a Chola village were called kudumbus.
Annual, garden and tank committees (variyams) managed village affairs.
The sabha had proprietary rights over communal land and collected land revenue.
Ur was the ordinary revenue-paying village.
Brahmadeya was a tax-free village granted to Brahmins.
Devadana was a village granted to a temple.
Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur.
Rajendra I defeated the Pala Mahipala and took the title Gangaikondachola.
Rajendra I built the new capital Gangaikondacholapuram.
Rajendra I's navy invaded the Srivijaya empire.
The Cholas sent diplomatic missions to China.
Kulottunga I united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas.
Kulottunga I was titled 'Sungam tavirtta' — he who abolished tolls.
Rajaraja II built the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram.
In the Dravidian style the tower over the sanctum is the vimana; gateways are gopuras.
The Cholas perfected lost-wax bronze casting; the Nataraja is its finest example.
Vishnuvardhana established Hoysala independence by defeating the Cholas and capturing Gangavadi.
Belur and Halebidu (Dorasamudra) were the Hoysala capitals.
Hoysala temples used soft soapstone, stood on a jagati platform and often had a stellate plan.
Veera Ballala III was killed in the Battle of Madurai (1343), ending the Hoysalas.
Bhillama V declared independence and made Devagiri the Yadava capital.
The Yadavas were among the first to adopt Marathi as an official language.
Malik Kafur defeated and captured Ramachandra in 1308.
Chalukya branches: Badami (Vatapi), Western Chalukyas of Kalyani and Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi.
The Kakatiyas declared independence from the Chalukyas in 1163 under Prataparudra I.
Hanumakonda was the first Kakatiya capital before Warangal.
Ganapati Deva created the Pakhal Lake and issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam.
Rudrama Devi was the first female Kakatiya ruler, praised by Marco Polo.
Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323, and Prataparudra II was captured.
The Ramappa (Rudreswara) temple was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
Pulakeshin I (c.543–566) founded the Chalukya kingdom of Badami, fortified Vatapi and performed the ashvamedha.
Kirtivarman I (566–597) defeated the Kadambas of Banavasi.
Mangalesha's inscription (578 CE) is in Cave 3 (the Vishnu cave) at Badami.
Pulakeshin II (610–642) was the greatest Badami Chalukya ruler.
Vikramaditya I (655–681) restored Chalukya power and recovered Vatapi from the Pallavas.
Vikramaditya II (733–744) occupied the Pallava capital Kanchi.
Kirtivarman II (744–753) was the last Badami Chalukya, overthrown by Dantidurga.
The Aihole inscription (634 CE) of Pulakeshin II was composed by his court poet Ravikirti.
Pulakeshin II defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada (c.618–619).
Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) visited the kingdom of Pulakeshin II.
Pulakeshin II exchanged embassies with the Persian king Khusrau II.
Pallava Narasimhavarman I killed Pulakeshin II, captured Vatapi (642) and took the title Vatapikonda.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakeshin II, founded the Eastern Chalukya line of Vengi in 624 CE.
Aihole, with about 120 temples, is called the cradle of Indian temple architecture.
Badami has four rock-cut cave temples — three Hindu and one Jain.
Pattadakal was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
Pattadakal has temples of both the Nagara (Papanatha) and Dravida (Virupaksha) styles side by side.
The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal was built by Queen Lokamahadevi to celebrate Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas.
The Mallikarjuna temple at Pattadakal was built by Queen Trailokyamahadevi.
The Chalukyan (Deccan) temple style that mixes Nagara and Dravida features is called Vesara.
Tailapa II founded the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani in 973 by overthrowing the Rashtrakuta Karka II.
Someshvara I made Kalyani (Basavakalyan) the capital.
Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126) started the Chalukya-Vikrama era in 1076.
Bilhana wrote the Vikramankadevacharita, a biography of Vikramaditya VI.
Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara, a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti and a basic text of Hindu inheritance law.
Someshvara III wrote the Manasollasa (Abhilashitartha Chintamani), an encyclopaedia.
The Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas rose as feudatories of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.
The Eastern Chalukyas ruled coastal Andhra from Vengi (near Eluru).
Nannaya began the Telugu Andhra Mahabharatam under Rajaraja Narendra.
Rajaraja Narendra married the Chola princess Ammangadevi, daughter of Rajendra I; their son became Kulottunga I.
Dantidurga left an inscription in the Dashavatara cave (Cave 15) at Ellora.
Dantidurga's daughter Reva married the Pallava king Nandivarman II, an ally against the Chalukyas.
Dhruva Dharavarsha (780–793) was the first Rashtrakuta to intervene in the north, defeating Vatsaraja and Dharmapala.
Amoghavarsha I ruled for about 64 years (814–878).
Amoghavarsha I also wrote the Sanskrit Prashnottara Ratnamalika.
Indra III (914–929) sacked Kanauj in 916, defeating the Pratihara Mahipala.
Krishna III defeated the Chola Parantaka I at the Battle of Takkolam (949).
The last Rashtrakuta, Karka II, was overthrown by Tailapa II in 973.
Ellora has 34 caves: 1–12 Buddhist, 13–29 Hindu and 30–34 Jain.
The Kailasa temple is Cave 16 at Ellora.
A Kailasa temple sculpture shows Ravana trying to lift Mount Kailasa.
The Elephanta caves (Mahesamurti) are usually credited to the Rashtrakutas, though some scholars credit the Kalachuris.
Pampa, called Adikavi, wrote the Kannada Adipurana and Vikramarjuna Vijaya.
Pampa, Ponna and Ranna are the three gems (Ratnatraya) of Kannada literature.
Ranna wrote the Gadayuddha.
The mathematician Mahaviracharya wrote the Ganitasarasangraha at the court of Amoghavarsha I.
Sakatayana wrote the Amoghavritti, a grammar.
Jinasena wrote the Parshvabhyudaya, a verse life of Parshvanatha.
The Rashtrakuta kingdom was divided into rashtras (provinces) under rashtrapatis, and vishayas (districts) under vishayapatis.
Arab writers called the Rashtrakuta king 'Balhara' (from Vallabharaja).
The Arab merchant Suleman (851 CE) ranked Amoghavarsha I among the four greatest kings of the world.
Bharuch (Broach) in Gujarat was the chief Rashtrakuta port for trade with the Arabs.
Vijayalaya (c.850) founded the Imperial Chola line by capturing Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars.
Aditya I defeated the Pallava Aparajita, ending Pallava power.
Parantaka I took the title 'Maduraikonda' after capturing Madurai.
Rajaraja I (985–1014) was originally named Arumolivarman.
Rajadhiraja I was killed in the Battle of Koppam (1054) against the Kalyani Chalukya Someshvara I.
Virarajendra defeated the Chalukyas and erected a pillar of victory on the banks of the Tungabhadra.
Kulottunga I ruled 1070–1122.
Rajaraja II built the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram.
Rajendra III (to 1279) was the last Chola; the Pandyas of Madurai replaced them.
After defeating Mahinda V of Ceylon, Rajaraja I made Polonnaruva the capital of the Chola province in Sri Lanka.
Rajaraja I annexed the Maldives.
Rajaraja I destroyed the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai.
The Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam was built by the Sailendra king Sri Mara Vijayottungavarman with Rajaraja I's encouragement.
Rajendra I took the title 'Kadaramkonda' after his naval raid on Kadaram (Kedah) in the Srivijaya empire.
Rajendra I defeated the Pala king Mahipala in 1022.
Rajendra I made the Pandya and Kerala lands a viceroyalty called Chola-Pandya with its headquarters at Madurai.
Kulottunga I sent an embassy of 72 merchants to China (1077).
Chola rule in Ceylon was ended by Vijayabahu I during Kulottunga I's reign.
Kulottunga I carried out a re-survey of land for revenue.
The Chola empire was divided into mandalams (provinces), then valanadus, nadus and villages (ur).
In the Chola system the nagaram was the assembly of merchants.
The ur was the general assembly of an ordinary (non-Brahmin) village.
The sabha (mahasabha) was the assembly of a Brahmadeya (Brahmin) village.
A large Brahmadeya village was called a chaturvedimangalam.
Uttaramerur is in Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu.
Uttaramerur village was divided into 30 wards (kudumbus).
The tank committee (eri-variyam) had six members.
Members of the mahasabha were called perunguri; committee members were variyapperumakkal.
The judicial committee of the village was called nyayattar.
Devadana villages became more popular under the Cholas as temples became centres of life.
Manigramam and Ayyavole (the Five Hundred) were major merchant guilds of the Chola age.
Sekkilar wrote the Periyapuranam (lives of the 63 Nayanars) under Kulottunga II.
Kamban wrote the Tamil Ramavataram (Kamba Ramayanam) in the Chola age.
Jayamkondar wrote the Kalingattupparani on Kulottunga I's Kalinga war.
Buddhamitra wrote the Tamil grammar Virasoliyam under Virarajendra.
Ottakuttan was the court poet of Vikrama Chola, Kulottunga II and Rajaraja II.
The Thanjavur Brihadisvara temple was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987; Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram were added in 2004.
The Thanjavur temple is called Dakshina Meru in its inscriptions.
The main gateway (gopura) of the Thanjavur temple is called Rajarajantiruvasal.
The walls of the Thanjavur temple carry Chola mural paintings.
The Gangaikondacholapuram temple (completed 1035) has a 53-m vimana with curving outlines, unlike the straight Thanjavur tower.
The Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram has a mandapa shaped like a chariot with wheels, an idea later expanded at Konark.
The Vijayalaya Cholisvaram temple is at Narthamalai.
The Brahmapurisvara temple is at Pullamangai.
Sala, the legendary founder of the Hoysalas, killed a tiger at his Jain guru's command; this is the Hoysala emblem.
Vishnuvardhana took the title 'Talakadugonda' after capturing Talakad from the Cholas (1116).
Vishnuvardhana was earlier called Bittideva.
Vishnuvardhana's queen Shantala Devi was a famed dancer and a Jain.
Veera Ballala II (1173–1220) fought the Yadavas and patronised the poet Janna.
The Keshava temple at Somanathapura was built in 1268 under Narasimha III.
Malik Kafur attacked the Hoysala capital Dwarasamudra in 1311 under Veera Ballala III.
The Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu (c.1121) was built by Ketamalla, an official of Vishnuvardhana.
The Chennakesava temple at Belur (1117) commemorates Vishnuvardhana's victory over the Cholas.
Hoysala temples are known for lathe-turned pillars.
The 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas' (Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
Hoysala administrative units were nadu, vishaya, kampana and desha.
Janna wrote the Yashodharacharite.
Harihara wrote the Girijakalyana.
Rudrabhatta wrote the Jagannatha Vijaya.
Dridhaprahara is the early (legendary) founder of the Seuna-Yadava family; Bhillama V founded the independent kingdom.
Bhillama V declared Yadava independence in 1187 and founded Devagiri.
Simhana II (c.1210–1247) was the greatest Yadava ruler.
Alauddin Khalji's raid on Devagiri in 1296, as governor of Kara under Jalaluddin, was the first Turkish raid into the Deccan.
Shankaradeva (Simhana III) was killed by Malik Kafur in 1313.
The last Yadava, Harapaladeva, was executed in 1318 under Mubarak Shah Khalji.
Sarangadeva wrote the Sangita Ratnakara, a key text of Indian music, at the court of Simhana II.
Hemadri (Hemadpant), minister of Mahadeva and Ramachandra, wrote the Chaturvarga Chintamani.
Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari (1290), a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, in Ramachandra's reign.
Mukundaraja wrote the Vivekasindhu, an early Marathi philosophical poem.
Mhaimbhat wrote the Lilacharitra, the Mahanubhava life of Chakradhar, an early Marathi prose work.
The Hemadpanti style uses local black stone fitted without mortar.
The Gondeshwar temple at Sinnar is a Bhumija-style Shiva temple with a panchayatana layout.
